catalog_quote: In Proto-Northern-Iroquoian, stress was basically penultimate, falling on the second-to-the-last syllable of the word. Closed stressed syllables remained short (CV), but open stressed syllables were lengthened. Stress patterns have changed drastically in Seneca and Cayuga, and certain other adjustments have been made in Onondaga, Oneida, and Mohawk. Some epenthetic vowels have been added in some of the languages, which did not affect stress placement or vowel length: original stressed vowels remain stressed, and original short vowels remain stressed. The Campanius vocabularies indicate that the original Proto-Northern-Iroquoian system remained essentially intact in Susquehannock. Stress was sometimes indicated with an accent mark and, as noted, length with double vowels. (14) Penultimate stress, closed syllables Áxe *áh.sę 'Three' Kássha *kás.ha 'Pass it to me' Tzátyę *Tsát.y[...] 'Sit down, you two' Uthíysta *o.tsís.ta? 'fire, coal, spark' Orócquæ *o.hrá.hkwa? 'meat' Serwquácksi *Se.rih.wák.si 'You are bad' Zwróncka *Sa.hrók.ha? 'You understand' (15) Penultimate stress, open syllables Hoona *ό:.nɛ 'now' Owntack *ý:.tak 'pot, kettle' Khaalis *ká:ris 'stockings' Kaatzie *ká:tsi 'Come here!' Chanoona *ka.nó:.na? 'tobacco pipe' Oneegha *oh.né:.ka?

new_statements.rule_in_words: Susquehannock retained the Proto-Northern-Iroquoian prosodic system: primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word; a stressed open (CV) penult is lengthened, a stressed closed penult stays short. Campanius' acute accents (Serɷquácksi, Zɷróncka) mark the stressed penult and his doubled vowels (Kaatzie, Khaalis, Hoona) mark the lengthened open stressed penult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing seen in the accessible snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: Mithun says PNI stress was 'basically' penultimate; epenthetic vowels (regular in Susquehannock, ex. (13): tiggene *tékeni 'two', waderom *wáʔteroʔ 'nine', katzera *kátsheraʔ 'clothing') 'did not affect stress placement or vowel length', so stress stays on the original vowel and surfaces as antepenultimate in words with an epenthetic penult.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress inferred philologically from a 1640s wordlist (accent marks and doubled vowels in Campanius 1696/Holm 1702) combined with comparative Northern Iroquoian evidence; forms are reconstituted (*starred) citation forms and short phrases. This is a reconstruction for a dormant language, not an observed description.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern the single attested variety: the 'Minque/Mahakuassica' vocabulary recorded by Johan Campanius among the Susquehannock (Conestoga/Andaste) near New Sweden in the 1640s (Campanius 1696; Holm 1702) = Glottolog susq1241. Mithun's 2023 statement is a comparative reconstitution (starred forms), i.e. the stress rule is inferred from Campanius' accent marks plus Proto-Northern-Iroquoian, not observed from speakers.
